A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching material across extensive reformatting and appendix renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original analyses of representation dimensionality, compositionality, and training dynamics on controlled grammatical stimuli and The Pile, including Figures 2–5 and Table 1.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical analyses and adds original results for Llama, Mistral, and varying sentence lengths, including Figure G.2 and Appendices I–J.

M1.justification: The coupling and shuffling procedure, last-token residual-stream representations, TwoNN estimator, PCA with 99% explained variance, and gzip analysis remain unchanged. Appendix E elaborates the existing sampling procedure; additional pretrained models are subjects of the same analysis.

E1.justification: v3 adds four shorter grammatical templates producing 5-, 8-, 11-, and 15-word sentences alongside the retained long template. This extends syntactic coverage within the same English compositionality task. The Pile and the seven checkpoint-evaluation benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: The dimensionality methods compared remain TwoNN, MLE, PCA, and Participation Ratio. Llama and Mistral are additional models whose representations are studied, rather than new competing methods evaluated against a proposed algorithm.

E3.justification: v3 substantially extends the evaluation design with Llama-3-8B and Mistral-v0.1-7B, sentence-length sweeps, and correlations pooled across grammars. The shortest-length comparison permits only coherent versus shuffled conditions (Table I.1). Section 3.2 also revises the stated long-template and Pile sequence length from 16 to 17 words; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test robustness across model families and sentence lengths, including whether shuffling feature collapse depends on length (Figures G.2 and J.1–J.3). Expanded Appendix I adds correlations across lengths and pooled layer distributions. These substantially extend v1's analyses of coupling, shuffling, alternative estimators, and training dynamics.

E5.justification: Five splits/seeds and reporting of ±1 SD are retained, with no documented increase in repetitions. The new Figure I.1 introduces significance markers at 0.01 and 0.001, while the existing tables retain 0.05/0.1 thresholds. Table I.1 also explicitly flags the two-observation limitation of five-word correlations.

E6.justification: Original Pythia entries in Table 1 and regression values in Tables G.1/H.1 are retained. Table 1 adds nonlinear/linear correlations of -0.36/1.00 for Llama and 0.00/1.00 for Mistral. Appendices I–J add extensive results, including near-zero shuffling gaps for five-word sentences. Table I.1's 17-word correlations differ from Table 1 without a clear explanation of aggregation differences.

T1.justification: The TwoNN assumptions and derivation, dimensionality inequality, Participation Ratio formula, and discrete-manifold qualification are retained. The additional sampling notation and standard explanation of Kolmogorov complexity elaborate existing concepts without introducing new theoretical results or proofs.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the four central claims: different linear/nonlinear scaling, geometry tracking linguistic emergence, nonlinear dimensionality shifting toward semantic complexity during training, and linear dimensionality encoding superficial complexity. The broader experiments support these retained claims rather than redefine the contributions.

C2.justification: v3 refines the explanation of when semantics-unaware gzip can proxy compositional complexity and interprets short-sentence representations as approaching bag-of-words complexity. It newly emphasizes that dimensionality does not identify the underlying features. Its added 8B model-size limitation conflicts with retained 12B results; the causal-mechanism caveat already existed.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds an explicit indexed procedure for uniformly sampling coupled vocabularies and specifies the four shorter grammar templates. Vocabulary lists, computing resources, runtime estimates, and asset links remain. Removing the standalone reproducibility statement does not remove its underlying technical information.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting information-theoretic framing, including Levy, Mollica and Piantadosi, and Elmoznino et al., alongside citations for the additional models. It removes several earlier references, including Hupkes et al., Chersoni et al., and Flesch et al. The central positioning relative to geometric compression and predictive coding remains; Cheng's 2024-to-2025 update concerns the same work.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and substantial portions of the methods, results, and discussion are rewritten. Terminology shifts from sane to coherent and emphasizes superficial versus meaningful complexity. The form–meaning analysis becomes a separate Section 5, appendices C/D exchange positions, and Appendix E gains a structured sampling explanation.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, with extensively resized figures, revised legends, and side-positioned captions. The original dataset diagram moves from Figure 1 to Figure E.1. Table 1 gains model columns, and new model-comparison, correlation, and sequence-length displays substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: The additional model-family and sentence-length checks strengthen the retained findings and reveal a useful short-sentence boundary. Clearer sampling instructions and qualifications also improve reproducibility and interpretation. These benefits are tempered by unexplained differences between Table 1 and Table I.1's 17-word correlations and the contradictory 8B limitation despite retained 12B results. The net improvement is positive but limited.
